lessons.title: Bulls that held up a roof

n1.text: Two bulls kneel back to back, carved in limestone. They once crowned a column of the great audience hall, the apadana, at Susa.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Look at the hollow between the two heads. Imagine what weight once rested there.

q1.text: What rested between the two heads?

choices.label: A bowl for a sacred fire

b1a.text: No statue: the bulls held up the building.

correction.tempting: A royal hall might show the king high up.
correction.truth: The two bulls carried the ceiling or roof beams between them.
correction.evidence: Encyclopaedia Iranica; Metropolitan Museum of Art.

b1b.text: Yes. The paired bulls carried the wooden beams of the ceiling or roof between them. The Louvre shows one laid on their backs.

b1c.text: No fire bowl: this was part of the roof's support.

correction.tempting: The hollow looks like a cradle for a bowl.
correction.truth: The two bulls carried the ceiling or roof beams between them.
correction.evidence: Encyclopaedia Iranica; Metropolitan Museum of Art.

n2.text: The hall was vast: 36 stone columns held up its roof, each about 20 metres tall.

q2.text: Where was this kind of capital invented?

b2a.text: Not Greece: the double-animal capital is Persian.

correction.tempting: Darius names Ionian stonecutters among his workers.
correction.truth: Scholars call the double-animal capital an Iranian invention, an entirely Achaemenid creation.
correction.evidence: Encyclopaedia Iranica; Metropolitan Museum of Art; the Louvre's 1992 Susa catalogue.

b2b.text: Not Egypt: the double-animal capital is Persian.

correction.tempting: Darius names Egyptians among his craftsmen.
correction.truth: Scholars call the double-animal capital an Iranian invention, an entirely Achaemenid creation.
correction.evidence: Encyclopaedia Iranica; Metropolitan Museum of Art; the Louvre's 1992 Susa catalogue.

b2c.text: Yes. Scholars call it an Iranian invention, an entirely Achaemenid creation, though its decoration took in ideas from the arts of the empire's many peoples.

n3.text: Darius wrote that the stone columns came from Elam, and that Ionians and Sardians cut the stone.

q3.text: An inscription says the hall burned. What do scholars make of it?

choices.label: They disagree how bad it was

b3a.text: The same inscription says the hall was restored.

correction.tempting: The inscription speaks of a fire.
correction.truth: Artaxerxes II's inscription says it burned and was restored. How badly it burned is debated.
correction.evidence: The Louvre's 1992 Susa catalogue; Encyclopaedia Iranica.

b3b.text: Yes. Artaxerxes II wrote that the hall burned and that he restored it. Some scholars think it was destroyed and rebuilt; others, that it needed only repairs.

b3c.text: The inscription does record a fire.

correction.tempting: The bulls survived to be found.
correction.truth: Artaxerxes II's inscription says the hall burned under Artaxerxes I and was restored.
correction.evidence: The Louvre's 1992 Susa catalogue; Encyclopaedia Iranica.

n6.text: Picture the whole building: a square hall with a tower at each corner and porches of twelve columns on three sides.

q5.text: Darius built a hall of this kind at Persepolis too. Which came first?

choices.label: Both at once, to one plan

b5a.text: The other way round: Susa came first.

correction.tempting: The Persepolis hall was also Darius's work.
correction.truth: The Louvre's 1992 catalogue calls the Persepolis hall a replica of Susa's; Stronach suggests Persepolis followed Susa's plan.
correction.evidence: The Louvre's 1992 Susa catalogue; Encyclopaedia Iranica (Stronach).

b5b.text: Not at once: Susa's plan was the model.

correction.tempting: The two halls share a square plan.
correction.truth: Susa's hall came first: the Louvre's 1992 catalogue calls the Persepolis hall a replica, and Stronach suggests Persepolis followed Susa's plan.
correction.evidence: The Louvre's 1992 Susa catalogue; Encyclopaedia Iranica (Stronach).

b5c.text: Yes. The Louvre's 1992 catalogue calls the Persepolis hall a replica of the one at Susa, and Stronach, in Encyclopaedia Iranica, suggests Persepolis followed Susa's innovative plan.

n4.text: Marcel Dieulafoy's French mission dug the bulls out in 1884–86 and shipped them to Paris, where they went on show in the Louvre.

q4.text: Where else can you see this kind of capital?

b4a.text: Yes. The facades of the Persian royal tombs cut into the rock, as at Naqsh-e Rostam, copy a columned palace, capitals included.

b4b.text: Not on Greek temples: this form is Persian.

correction.tempting: The scrolls below the bulls recall Greek columns.
correction.truth: The form is Persian; it is carved on the rock-cut royal tombs, as at Naqsh-e Rostam.
correction.evidence: Encyclopaedia Iranica; the Louvre's 1992 Susa catalogue; Jane Dieulafoy (1888).

b4c.text: Not on obelisks: this form is Persian.

correction.truth: It is carved on the facades of the Persian rock-cut royal tombs, as at Naqsh-e Rostam.
correction.evidence: Encyclopaedia Iranica; the Louvre's 1992 Susa catalogue; Jane Dieulafoy (1888).

n7.text: The French were not the first to dig here. In the early 1850s the geologist William Kennett Loftus had already recognised the apadana.

q6.text: Dieulafoy published a restored plan of the buildings. How do scholars judge it?

choices.label: A careful record of what survived

b6a.text: Not a careful record: scholars call it speculative.

correction.tempting: A plan drawn by the excavator himself sounds reliable.
correction.truth: Robert Dyson called it possibly one of the greatest speculative tours de force in archaeology.

b6b.text: Yes. Robert Dyson wrote that Dieulafoy's bias toward architecture warped the evidence, and called his plan possibly one of the greatest speculative tours de force in archaeology.

b6c.text: Not proven: later scholars call it speculative.

correction.tempting: Excavations at Susa went on for decades after him.
correction.truth: Later scholars judge his plan speculative; Hermann Gasche speaks of his occasionally fantastic reconstructions.

n5.text: Bulls that held up a king's roof, now under a museum ceiling. They stand in Room 307, on Floor 0 of the Sully wing.

lessons.takeaway: Two limestone bulls that crowned a column of the audience hall at Susa, the model for Persepolis: they carried the roof beams, the double-animal capital is a Persian invention, how badly the hall burned is still debated, and Dieulafoy's restored plan is bold but speculative.
